paragraphs: A spilled product is a different asset from a packaged one. The box lies open, the mints scatter across the surface in a loose arc, and a few rest against each other rather than sitting in a tidy pile. That disorder is the point: it implies motion and use, which a closed box on a white background never does.

The mesh is efficient at 15,612 polygons and 15,663 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 6 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the box printing and the slightly translucent sugar shell of the mints.

At $29 and built to StemCell specification, it suits confectionery advertising, packaging and brand mockups, retail and e-commerce renders, food photography set dressing and games. On sale since 2021.

Sports eyewear is built around a single wraparound lens rather than two, with the frame reduced to a brow bar and temple arms so nothing blocks peripheral vision. That construction is what distinguishes it from ordinary sunglasses, and this set gives several designs, which matters because a team or a group scene needs variety rather than the same frame repeated.

The meshes together are minimal at 4,332 polygons and 4,328 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which is right for eyewear: the geometry is thin, and the character comes from the lens material and the tint.

At $29 it suits sports advertising, eyewear retail and catalogue renders, character set dressing for film, television and games, and outdoor activity visualisation. On sale since 2015, kept to real-world scale so they fit a standard head.

A bulkhead light is a marine fitting that became an interior design staple: a heavy cast body, a threaded glass dome and a protective cage over it, all built to survive a deck. The corrugated glass is the detail that makes it work indoors, because it breaks the bulb into a pattern instead of glaring.

The mesh is 24,134 polygons and 12,359 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the glass modelled as its own body so a refractive material can produce the ribbed light pattern rather than faking it.
At $29 it suits interior and hospitality visualisation, industrial and nautical styling, exterior and marine scenes, lighting retail renders and games. On sale since 2023.

A quarter is a small object photographed at enormous magnification, which is why the relief matters more than anything else. The portrait, the lettering and the reeded edge all have to be real depth rather than a bump map, because the whole reason a coin reads as metal is the way light catches those raised edges.

The mesh is minimal at 2,908 polygons and 2,910 vertices, built entirely from quads with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 5 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the relief detail and the worn nickel finish.

At $29 and built to StemCell specification, it suits financial and banking visualisation, advertising, product and packaging renders, scale references, games and print. On sale since 2015, kept to real-world scale so it sits correctly beside a hand or another object.

A swim cap is a stretched membrane over a head, and its whole character comes from that tension: it pulls smooth over the crown, gathers into a rolled edge at the brow and creases slightly behind the ears. Modelled as a rigid dome it looks like a helmet rather than silicone.

The mesh is minimal at 1,936 polygons and 1,938 vertices, built entirely from quads with non-overlapping UVs. All-quad geometry matters on a stretched surface, since it deforms cleanly when fitted to different head shapes.

At $29 it suits swimming and aquatic sports visualisation, sports broadcast graphics, swimwear retail renders, character set dressing for games and film, and advertising. On sale since 2021, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard head.

An autonomous sweeper has no cab, and losing the cab changes the whole machine: the body drops low, the sensors go on a mast where a driver's eyes would have been, and the brush and suction gear take up the space a person used to occupy. That absence is the visual argument for the technology, and it is what makes the vehicle interesting in a render.
The mesh is efficient at 51,355 polygons and 54,468 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the detail in the sensor mast, the brush heads and the hopper.

At $24 and built to StemCell specification, it suits smart city and municipal visualisation, autonomous vehicle marketing, sustainability and clean technology presentation, urban scenes and games. On sale since 2024.

A gate valve closes by lowering a flat wedge across the flow, which is why it has a tall bonnet and a rising stem under the handwheel - the stem needs somewhere to go. The hexagonal body flats, the threaded ends and the cast markings are the other identifying features, and this model builds them rather than smoothing the body into a tube.
The mesh is light at 6,323 polygons and 6,299 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the handwheel spokes, the bonnet and the thread ends.

At $24 it suits plumbing and building services visualisation, industrial and process piping scenes, equipment catalogues, technical and training material, and games. On sale since 2023, kept to real-world scale so it fits standard pipework.

A cardboard box is one of the most useful props in existence, and the useful ones are never pristine. The flaps cross at the top or stand open, the corners round out slightly under weight, and the printed handling symbols sit where the manufacturer put them rather than where a designer would.

The mesh is minimal at 6,506 polygons and 3,257 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. Boxes appear in stacks, in rooms and in warehouses, so the low weight matters more than surface complexity, which the texture supplies anyway.

At $24 it suits moving and relocation visualisation, warehouse and logistics scenes, interior renders, retail and e-commerce packaging, film and television set dressing, and games. On sale since 2024.

A champagne bucket is a hospitality signal as much as a container: polished metal, ring handles, a flared rim and a base narrow enough to sit in a stand. Including the ice picks changes what the set can show, because tongs and a pick beside the bucket say service in progress rather than an object on a table.
The mesh is light at 4,281 polygons and 4,264 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits objects whose interest comes almost entirely from a reflective metal material.

At $24 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits restaurant and hospitality visualisation, beverage and luxury advertising, event and celebration renders, bar interiors and games. On sale since 2025.

A hotel housekeeping cart is a mobile store cupboard: shelves for linen, a bag for laundry hanging off one end, a bin at the other and a top tray for amenities. The clutter is what makes it read correctly - an empty cart looks like a shelving unit on wheels and tells a viewer nothing about the space it stands in.

The mesh runs 106,004 polygons and 54,785 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the frame, the castors and the bag frame where a close camera lands in a corridor scene.
At $24 it suits hotel and hospitality visualisation, facility management presentation, interior renders, film and television set dressing, and games. On sale since 2023.

The ten shekel coin is bimetallic, a nickel ring around a golden centre, and that two-tone construction is the first thing anyone notices. The join between the metals has to be a real edge with its own reflectance, because a single-material coin with a printed ring reads as a token rather than as currency.
The mesh is minimal at 1,844 polygons and 924 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the relief and the reeded segments carried where the light needs an edge to catch.

At $24 it suits financial and banking visualisation, currency and exchange material, advertising, product renders, scale reference and games. On sale since 2024, kept to real-world scale so it sits correctly beside a hand or a wallet.

The one shekel coin is a plain nickel disc with a smooth edge and a lily emblem on the reverse, and plainness is harder to model well than complexity: there is no ornament to distract the eye from a wrong relief depth or a rim that is too sharp.

The mesh is minimal at 1,152 polygons and 578 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which is exactly the right economy for a small object whose realism comes from material rather than from geometry.

At $24 it suits financial and banking visualisation, currency material, advertising and product renders, scale references and games. On sale since 2024, kept to real-world scale so it reads correctly in a pile of change or a hand.

A cardboard lemonade stand is a specific kind of object: flat panels slotted together, hand-lettered signage, and the slight sag that cardboard takes when it stands up as furniture. That imperfection is the whole charm, and a crisply rendered kiosk reads as a shop rather than as something a child built.
The mesh is efficient at 17,610 polygons and 17,564 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the panel edges and the slot joints where the construction shows.
At $24 it suits children's and family advertising, summer and seasonal material, packaging and toy visualisation, editorial illustration, and games. On sale since 2022.

A cream separator is a centrifuge dressed as a kitchen appliance: a bowl on top that holds the milk, a spinning drum inside, and two spouts at different heights so cream comes out one and skimmed milk the other. Those twin spouts are the identifying feature, and the model builds them along with the bowl and the motor housing.
The mesh is 22,808 polygons and 11,434 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the milk modelled so the bowl reads as full rather than as an empty vessel.
At $24 it suits dairy and food industry visualisation, farm and smallholding scenes, appliance retail and catalogue renders, food processing presentation and games. On sale since 2022.
